title: Stand on a disc in St Peter’s Square and Bernini’s four rows of columns become one
body: Gian Lorenzo Bernini built the colonnades of [St Peter’s Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Peter%27s_Square) in 1656–1667 for Pope Alexander VII: 284 columns and 88 pillars, four rows deep, curving round an oval. Between the obelisk and each fountain, a round stone in the paving reads *Centro del colonnato*, centre of the colonnade. Stand on one and face the nearer colonnade, and its four rows close up into one, as the [Vatican’s own page](https://www.vatican.va/content/vatican/en/ra/piastrelle-centro-del-colonnato.html) describes. The reason is geometry: the rows are **arcs of circles centred on that disc**, and each set of four columns stands on one radius, so every line of sight from the disc runs along a set and the front column hides the three behind. From anywhere else the sight lines cut across the sets. The discs are often called the oval’s foci, but [a 2026 preprint](https://www.researchsquare.com/article/rs-10455562/v1), building on earlier surveys, describes an *ovato tondo*: two circles round the discs, about 66 m apart, joined by two wider arcs into a near-ellipse.

slides.question: Architect Gian Lorenzo Bernini’s colonnades round St Peter’s Square are four rows deep. How many columns do they have?
slides.explanation: 284 columns and 88 pillars, the Vatican says, built in 1656–1667. 140 statues of saints, about 3 m tall, stand along the top.

slides.alt: Animation on a dark plum ground: a plan of St Peter’s Square with its oval, obelisk, fountains and two four-row colonnades. A view panel shows the columns from a walker’s eye, a jumble of rows, then one clean row from the disc. Sight lines run from the disc along each set; circles make the oval.

slides.prompt: Walk round St Peter’s Square and find the spot where no back-row column of Bernini’s north colonnade shows.
slides.takeaway: Only on the disc, the centre of the colonnade’s circles, does every set of four line up, because each sight line runs along a radius. From the obelisk or anywhere else, dozens of back-row columns peek out.

slides.alt: Close-up of a round white marble plaque set in the dark cobbles of St Peter’s Square, with a grey stone disc in the middle and the words CENTRO DEL COLONNATO carved round the ring.
slides.caption: One of the two discs, set in the cobbles between the obelisk and a fountain.

slides.heading: Why the four rows line up

steps.label: Each colonnade is an arc of a circle
The disc marks that circle’s centre
Each set of four columns lies on one radius
From the disc, sight lines run along sets
The front column hides the three behind

left.label: Often said
left.text: The square is an ellipse, and the discs mark its two foci.

right.label: The geometry
right.text: The plan is an oval of circle arcs, and each disc is the centre of its colonnade’s circles. That is what lines up the rows.

slides.question: On the disc between the obelisk and the north fountain of St Peter’s Square, which colonnade’s four rows close up into one?
options: The south one, across the square
slides.explanation: Each disc is the centre of the nearer colonnade’s circles. From it, the far colonnade’s sets point elsewhere, so its rows still show: its own disc is on the other side of the obelisk.

source.label: Vatican: Centre of the colonnade, St Peter’s Square
